topics.name: Malaysia student visa: the 5 steps
facts: Step 1: get an offer letter from a recognised Malaysian university or college.

Step 2: the student pass (visa) application is made through EMGS (Education Malaysia Global Services); usually the university submits it, and the student must be outside Malaysia (in the home country) while it is processed.
Step 3: after approval the student gets an eVAL (electronic Visa Approval Letter).
Step 4: students from countries that need a visa, such as Pakistan and India, take the eVAL to the Malaysian embassy or high commission and get a Single Entry Visa (SEV).
Step 5: after arriving in Malaysia, do the medical screening at an EMGS panel clinic within 7 days, then the student pass is endorsed (stuck) in the passport.
The eVAL is valid for 6 months from the date of approval; enter Malaysia before it expires.
Processing time is several weeks, so apply early.

topics.name: Do not come on a tourist visa to get a student pass
facts: A tourist (social visit) pass cannot be converted into a student pass.
You must get the student pass approval (eVAL) before entering Malaysia; the application is processed while you are outside Malaysia.
If you enter Malaysia on a social pass while waiting, you may be asked to leave and re-enter with the Visa Approval Letter.
Being in Malaysia on a visit visa during the application can cause delays or rejection.

topics.name: What to do after landing in Malaysia
facts: Bring your passport, the eVAL and the EMGS approval letter, and your Single Entry Visa if your country needs one.
Most international students also need to fill the Malaysia Digital Arrival Card (MDAC) before entering Malaysia.
Do the post-arrival medical screening at an EMGS panel clinic within 7 days of arrival.
Register at your university, then the student pass sticker is endorsed in your passport.
After the student pass is endorsed you get the i-Kad (international student card).

topics.name: Part-time work rules for international students
facts: International students may work part-time for a maximum of 20 hours per week.
Work is allowed only during semester breaks or holidays of more than 7 days, not during normal study weeks.
Allowed places include restaurants, petrol stations, mini markets and hotels.
You need approval from the Immigration Department; the application is made through your university, with a support letter showing your semester and holiday dates.
Your student pass must stay valid; working without approval is not allowed.

topics.name: What is the i-Kad
facts: The i-Kad is a biometric identification card for international students, issued after the student pass is endorsed.
It is handled through EMGS together with the student pass; you do not apply for it separately.
It is a valid ID in Peninsular Malaysia, so you can keep your passport safe at home.
It is not a travel document: you still need your passport to travel abroad or to Sabah and Sarawak (East Malaysia).
If you lose it, a police report is needed to apply for a replacement.

topics.name: Student pass renewal: do not be late
facts: The student pass must be renewed before it expires (usually every year, or as given on your pass).
Your university can start the renewal up to 3 months before the expiry date.
EMGS recommends submitting the renewal no later than 6 weeks before expiry.
Late renewal brings extra fines or a special pass fee.
After the pass expires it cannot be renewed; you must apply for a new eVAL from outside Malaysia.
Insurance bought through EMGS must also be renewed every year.

topics.name: Can you work in Malaysia after graduation? Graduate Pass
facts: The Graduate Pass is a Social Visit Pass that lets international graduates of Malaysian universities stay for up to 12 months after graduation.
With the Graduate Pass you can look for work and work without needing an employer to sponsor you.
The Graduate Pass is only for eligible nationalities, so check EMGS for your country before you plan on it.
For a longer job you need an Employment Pass; one category for foreign graduates of Malaysian institutions allows up to 24 months.
Plan your job search before your student pass ends.

topics.name: Malaysia International Scholarship (MIS) for Master's and PhD
facts: The Malaysia International Scholarship (MIS) is a Malaysian Government scholarship for full-time Master's and PhD study.
It pays the tuition fees directly to the university and gives a monthly living allowance of RM1,500.
Only citizens of the MIS recipient countries can apply, so check the yearly list of countries.
In 2026 the application was open from 4 March to 3 April, so watch for the next call early in the year.
Applicants submit a research proposal of at least 1,000 words; for a Master's the applicant must not be older than 40.
Applications are made online on the Ministry of Higher Education scholarship website (biasiswa.mohe.gov.my).

topics.name: Student visa fees are not the same at every university
facts: The student pass and visa processing fee is paid to EMGS, usually through your university.
The amount is different at each university and depends on your level of study and nationality.
Example: Sunway University lists RM2,400 for the student pass and visa processing fee.
Example: University of Cyberjaya lists RM2,200; its fee includes EMGS processing, medical insurance, health examination, i-Kad and a multiple-entry visa.
Some universities also take a visa deposit; for example Nottingham Malaysia asks RM2,000, refunded after the student pass is cancelled at the end of studies.
EMGS fees are not refunded if the visa is rejected, so ask your university for the exact total before you pay.

topics.name: Documents needed for the student visa
facts: Offer letter from the Malaysian university or college.
Passport: copy of the pages; universities usually ask for long validity (some ask for more than 18 months).
Passport-size photo with a white background (35mm x 45mm).
Academic transcripts and certificates.
Proof of English (for example IELTS or TOEFL) if your course asks for it.
A completed Health Declaration Form.
Fees paid to EMGS and the immigration are not refunded if the eVAL is rejected, so check every document carefully.

topics.name: When to apply: intakes
facts: Public universities usually have 2 intakes: September/October (main) and February/March.
Many private universities have more intakes, for example January, May and September.
Exact dates differ by university and course, so check the university website.
Apply early: some universities ask for all documents at least 8 weeks before the intake, because the visa also takes weeks.

topics.name: Student living cost in Malaysia
facts: Monthly cost depends on the city, the type of accommodation and your lifestyle.
Accommodation is usually the biggest monthly expense; on-campus hostel is usually the cheapest option.
Kuala Lumpur is usually more expensive than cities like Penang or Johor Bahru.
A simple local meal costs about RM5 to RM15.
Make a monthly budget before you come: rent, food, transport, phone and internet.

topics.name: Foundation year: the route after FSc / A-Levels
facts: A foundation programme is a pre-university course that prepares students for a bachelor's degree.
Most foundation programmes in Malaysia take about 1 year (2 or 3 semesters).
After the foundation you go straight into year 1 of a bachelor's degree, often at the same university.
A diploma is a different route: it usually takes 2 to 3 years and is more job-focused.
Entry requirements and English scores differ by university and course, so check the university page.

topics.name: Halal food and Muslim-friendly student life
facts: Malaysia describes itself as a modern, Muslim-friendly country with easy access to halal food.
Halal food is available almost everywhere, and many restaurants in big cities are open 24 hours.
Prayer facilities are common, including on campuses and in shopping malls.
Malaysia is multicultural: Malay, Chinese and Indian communities live together, with festivals throughout the year.
A simple local meal costs about RM5 to RM15.

topics.name: Can you bring your family? Dependant pass rules
facts: Students at Certificate or Diploma level are not allowed to bring dependants.
A Dependant Pass can be applied through EMGS only for immediate family: parents, spouse and children.
Immigration gives dependants a Long Term Social Visit Pass for a maximum of 12 months at a time.
Children below 18 can stay and study in Malaysia on a dependant pass; at 18 and above they need their own student pass.
Postgraduate students from all countries can apply for dependants; at undergraduate level only students from certain countries are allowed, so check with your university.
Universities advise bringing family only after your own Student Pass is endorsed, not on your first entry.

topics.name: Medical insurance for international students
facts: Medical insurance is compulsory for every international student in Malaysia to get the student pass.
The insurance must be bought locally in Malaysia, through EMGS or your university's approved insurer.
Even if your visa is for 2 or 3 years, the insurance must be renewed every year.
With insurance you are covered at clinics and hospitals listed on your plan (panel clinics).
To see a specialist you usually need a referral letter from a panel clinic doctor first.
New students do a medical screening at a panel clinic within 7 working days of arrival; renewing students do not need it again.

topics.name: Do you need to learn Malay? Language in Malaysia
facts: The official language of Malaysia is Bahasa Malaysia (Malay).
English is widely spoken in daily life: shops, transport and public services.
Most university courses for international students are taught in English.
You will also hear Mandarin, Tamil and other languages because Malaysia is multicultural.
Learning a few Malay words like 'terima kasih' (thank you) helps you make friends.

topics.name: International students can only study full time
facts: Under current rules, international students can only enrol in full-time courses (except mobility programmes).
A student pass is for study at an approved institution; it does not allow normal full-time work.
Part-time work is only allowed in semester breaks or holidays of more than 7 days, up to 20 hours a week, with approval.

topics.name: Public, private and international branch campuses
facts: Malaysia has public universities, private universities and branch campuses of foreign universities.
Examples of foreign branch campuses in Malaysia are Monash University Malaysia and the University of Nottingham Malaysia.
Many programmes are taught in English.
Public universities usually have fewer intakes than private universities.

topics.name: Common mistakes that can ruin your Malaysia study plan
facts: Coming on a tourist visa and hoping to change it to a student pass: this is not allowed.
Applying late: the visa takes weeks, so apply well before the intake.
Wrong or missing documents: EMGS and immigration fees are not refunded if the eVAL is rejected.
Missing the 7-day medical screening after arrival.
Working during study weeks: part-time work is only allowed in breaks of more than 7 days, up to 20 hours a week, with approval.
Renewing the student pass late: after it expires you need a new eVAL from outside Malaysia.
